prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

She awoke to find her fishtail clean gone but in the bed with her were two long, cold thingammies. You'd have thought they were tangles of kelp or collops of ham. "They're no doubt taking the piss, it being New Year's Eve. Half the staff legless with drink and the other half playing pranks. Still, this is taking it a bit far." And with that she hurled the two thingammies out of the room. But here's the thing she still doesn't get— why she tumbled out after them arse-over-tip... How she was connected to those two thingammies and how they were connected to her. It was the sister who gave her the wink and let her know what was what. "You have one leg attached to you there and another one underneath that. One leg, two legs... A-one and a-two... Now you have to learn what they can do." In the long months that followed, I wonder if her heart fell the way her arches fell, her instep arches.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- She woke up to discover that her fishtail had disappeared and been replaced by two strange, cold appendages.
- She assumed the staff were playing a drunken New Year’s Eve prank and threw the strange appendages out of the room.
- She did not yet understand that the appendages were actually her own legs and that she was physically connected to them.
- Her sister explained that she now had two legs and needed to learn how to use them.
- The text suggests that learning to live with legs was a long and emotionally painful process.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A mermaid-like woman wakes to find her tail replaced by two unfamiliar legs, and through her sister’s explanation she begins the difficult process of understanding and learning to use them. The passage reveals bodily transformation as disorienting and painful, emphasizing the emotional cost of adapting to a new human form.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: She, You, They

outputs.L1:
She awoke to discover that her fishtail had vanished entirely, and that in the bed beside her lay two long, cold appendages. One might have taken them for tangles of kelp, or slabs of ham. “They are no doubt taking the piss, it being New Year’s Eve: half the staff legless with drink and the other half playing pranks. Still, this is taking matters rather too far.” With that, she hurled the two appendages out of the room.

But here is the thing she still does not understand: why she tumbled out after them, arse-over-tip; how she was connected to those two appendages, and how they were connected to her. It was the sister who gave her the wink and told her what was what. “You have one leg attached to you there, and another one beneath it. One leg, two legs—one and two. Now you must learn what they can do.”

In the long months that followed, I wonder whether her heart fell as her arches fell—her instep arches.
outputs.L2:
She woke up and discovered that her fishtail had vanished completely. In the bed beside her lay two long, chilly objects. At first glance, they might have been clumps of seaweed or slabs of ham. “They must be having me on because it’s New Year’s Eve,” she thought. “Half the servants are drunk, and the rest are busy with practical jokes. Even so, this is going too far.” With that, she flung the two objects out of the room.

What she still cannot understand, though, is why she toppled after them, head over heels—how those two strange things were fastened to her, and how she was fastened to them. It was her sister who hinted at the truth and explained the situation. “There is one leg joined to you here, and another one below it. One leg, two legs… one and two… Now you must find out what they are able to do.”

During the many months that came afterward, I wonder whether her spirits sank just as her arches did—the arches of her feet.
outputs.L3:
When she woke, the first thing she noticed was that something was terribly wrong. Her familiar fishtail was gone. In its place were two strange, cold appendages that seemed completely foreign to her. They lay where her tail should have been, pale and awkward, and she stared at them in confusion and alarm, unable to understand what had happened to her body.

At first, she assumed it had to be some kind of joke. It was New Year’s Eve, after all, and she imagined that the staff must have become drunk and decided to play a cruel prank on her while she slept. Angry and frightened, she tried to rid herself of the bizarre things, treating them as though they were objects that had been left in her room. In her panic, she threw the strange appendages away from her, not realizing that they were not separate from her at all.

She did not yet understand that these unfamiliar limbs were actually her own legs. She had no concept of being connected to them or of needing them to move. To her, they were alien and unsettling, a shocking replacement for the graceful fishtail she had always known.

It was her sister who finally explained the truth. Gently but firmly, she told her that the appendages were now part of her body: she had two legs, and she would have to learn how to use them. This revelation marked the beginning of a difficult new stage in her life.

Learning to live with legs was not simple or easy. The change was not only physical but emotional. She had to adjust to a body that felt unfamiliar, clumsy, and painful, while also mourning the loss of the tail that had once defined her. The text suggests that this process took a long time and caused her great distress, as she struggled to accept and inhabit a form that felt strange and unnatural to her.
outputs.L4:
She woke to a heaviness she did not understand.

At first she thought she was still dreaming beneath the tide, wrapped in the soft pressure of deep water, her body rocked by currents and blue shadow. But there was no water around her. No salt on her tongue. No familiar pull of the sea lifting her gently and setting her down again. Instead, she lay on a bed of dry woven reeds, covered with a pale cloth that scratched strangely against her skin.

She tried to move her tail.

Pain flashed through her.

Her eyes flew open.

Where the long silver sweep of her tail should have been, there were two unfamiliar shapes beneath the cloth. They lay side by side, pale and separate, ending in narrow, delicate things that twitched when she stared at them. For a moment she could not understand what she was seeing. Her mind reached for the shape of herself—the strong curve of scales, the fin that had carried her through dark water, the muscle that had known every current. But that body was gone.

In its place were legs.

She drew in a sharp breath and tried to sit up. The movement sent a burning ache through her hips, as though her body had been split and remade while she slept. She pulled the cloth away with trembling hands. The two limbs shifted clumsily, no longer joined, no longer shining with scales. They were soft-skinned and strange, bending at places she did not know how to command.

“No,” she whispered.

Her voice sounded small in the dry air.

A figure moved beside her. Her sister was sitting near the bed, eyes red from weeping, her dark hair tangled over her shoulders. She reached out quickly, but stopped before touching her, as if afraid even comfort might hurt.

“You’re awake,” her sister said.

“What happened to me?” the woman asked. Her gaze remained fixed on the alien limbs. “Where is my tail?”

Her sister swallowed. “It changed.”

“That is not an answer.”

“I know.” Her sister’s voice broke. “I know it isn’t.”

The woman tried again to move, desperate now, needing to prove that her true body was hidden somehow beneath illusion. She pressed her palms into the bed and pushed herself upright. The legs jerked apart. One knee bent sharply; the other dragged uselessly. A cry escaped her before she could stop it.

Her sister caught her shoulders. “Careful. You must go slowly.”

“Slowly?” she said, almost laughing, though the sound came out ragged. “I do not even know what these are.”

“They are legs,” her sister said gently. “Human legs.”

The word human settled heavily between them.

She looked down again. Human. She had seen them before from the surface: sailors balancing on wooden decks, children running along moonlit beaches, women kneeling to gather shells. Their legs had seemed simple then, awkward but useful, little divided stems carrying them over the land. She had never imagined what it would feel like to have them. She had never imagined the terrible wrongness of being separated from herself.

“How do they move?” she asked.

Her sister shifted closer. “Not like a tail. You do not push with the whole body. Each leg moves apart from the other. These bend here”—she touched her own knee—“and here.” She pointed to her ankle. “The feet touch the ground. They carry your weight.”

“My weight,” the woman repeated.

In the sea, weight was something shared. The water held her. Even when she dove deep, even when pressure closed around her ribs, she belonged to it. Her body had been made for suspension, for gliding, for turning with a flick of muscle. But now the air pressed differently. The bed pressed against her. Her own bones seemed too present, too sharp, too heavy.

Her sister rose and held out both hands. “We can try to stand.”

The woman stared at her. “Now?”

“If you are able. Just for a moment.”

“I am not able.”

“You may not be,” her sister admitted. “But you will not know until you try.”

Anger rose in her, sudden and hot. “You speak as though this is some small lesson. As though I have misplaced a comb and must learn to braid my hair differently.”

Her sister flinched.

The anger vanished almost at once, leaving only fear behind. The woman looked away. “Forgive me.”

“There is nothing to forgive.”

“There is everything to forgive,” she whispered. “I do not know what I am.”

Her sister sat beside her again, and this time she took her hand. “You are still yourself.”

But the woman could not believe it. Herself had been swift. Herself had known the language of waves and the taste of distance. Herself had slept in caves of coral and risen through green light toward the silver skin of the world. Herself had a tail that flashed like a blade when she swam.

These legs did not feel like herself. They felt like a punishment. Like a bargain made in a language she had not fully understood.

Still, her sister waited.

At last the woman nodded.

Her sister helped her turn toward the edge of the bed. The movement was clumsy and humiliating. Her legs slid and tangled, bumping against each other as though they belonged to someone else. When her feet finally touched the floor, she gasped.

The ground was cold.

Not cool like deep water, not alive with movement, but hard and still. It did not yield. It did not welcome her. Her toes curled instinctively away from it.

“Put them flat,” her sister said softly. “Like this.”

She showed her with her own feet. The woman tried to copy the shape, spreading the unfamiliar soles against the floor. The sensation was overwhelming: pressure in her heels, a strange stretch in the arches, the tiny bones of her toes trembling under the effort of balance.

Her sister took both her hands. “Now lean forward.”

“I will fall.”

“I have you.”

“You cannot hold all of me.”

“I can hold enough.”

The woman drew a breath. She leaned forward.

For one brief moment, her weight shifted onto her feet.

Then pain tore upward through both legs.

She cried out and collapsed against her sister, shaking. Her knees buckled; her feet slipped; the room tilted wildly. Her sister lowered her carefully back onto the bed, murmuring apologies, but the woman barely heard them. She pressed her hands over her mouth, trying to stop the sob that rose inside her.

It was not only the pain. Pain she had known before: cuts from coral, the sting of jellyfish, the crushing cold of deep currents. This was different. This pain came from attempting to exist. From asking her new body to do what human bodies did without thought.

Her sister knelt before her, still holding her hands. “It will become easier.”

“When?”

“I do not know.”

The honesty hurt more than a lie would have.

The woman looked toward the open window. Beyond it, she could hear the sea. The tide moved somewhere below the cliffs, breathing against the rocks. The sound reached into her like a memory and pulled. She imagined slipping from the bed, dragging herself across the floor, down the path, over the stones, until the water closed over her head. But what would happen then? Would these legs kick helplessly? Would she sink? Would the sea know her now?

Tears blurred her sight.

“I want to go home,” she said.

Her sister bowed her head. “I know.”

“No,” the woman said, her voice cracking. “You do not know. You can still swim.”

Her sister did not answer.

For a while they sat in silence, the transformed woman on the edge of the bed and her sister kneeling at her feet. The new legs lay between them like a truth neither could soften. Slowly, carefully, her sister began to explain again: how the hips turned, how knees bent, how feet must be placed one before the other. She spoke of balance, of practice, of pain that might lessen but would not disappear all at once.

The woman listened, though each word felt like another stone added to her chest.

She understood then that waking had not been the end of the transformation. It was only the beginning. The change had given her a human shape, but not a human ease. She would have to learn every small motion. Sitting. Standing. Walking. She would have to endure the shame of falling, the ache of muscles that had never been used, the grief of remembering what it had once meant to move without thought.

Her sister touched her knee gently. “Again?” she asked.

The woman closed her eyes.

In the dark behind her lids, she saw the sea: endless, glittering, open. She saw herself cutting through it, whole and certain. Then she opened her eyes and saw the room, the floor, the two trembling legs that were now hers.

She was not ready.

But the world had changed without waiting for her readiness.

So she took her sister’s hands again.
outputs.L5:
She walks into the room carrying stories no one has heard yet. You notice the quiet confidence in her steps, the way she seems to understand more than she says. They whisper, they wonder, they try to guess who she is and where she has been.

But you know that people are never just what others decide about them. She is not only a face in the crowd. You are not only an observer. They are not only voices in the background.

Together, she, you, and they create the world around you — a world made of choices, memories, questions, and connections. She may inspire you. You may change them. They may shape the path ahead.

In the end, every story begins with someone: she, you, or they. And sometimes, the most important story is the one you decide to tell.

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite the scene where the Little Mermaid wakes up with human legs, but in a bawdy Irish comic voice, making her initially think the legs are some kind of prank.
counterfactuals.output:
When the little mermaid came to herself, she was lying on the pale sand just beyond the reach of the tide, with the morning sun warming her face and the sea whispering behind her like an old aunt pretending she hadn’t been listening.

For a moment she only blinked at the sky.

Then she tried to flick her tail.

Nothing happened.

She tried again, with more authority, the way one might persuade a lazy servant or a stubborn clam.

Still nothing.

She lifted her head.

And there, where her splendid silver fish-tail ought to have been—her pride, her glory, her sleek and shining instrument of swiftness—were two long, pale, ridiculous things, stuck out in front of her like a pair of badly peeled eels.

The little mermaid stared.

Then she screamed.

Not a grand oceanic scream, mind you—not the kind that sends dolphins scattering and makes sea-witches look up from their pots. No, this was a raw, indignant, land-creature sort of shriek.

“What in the name of seven drowned kings is this?”

She poked one of the things.

It twitched.

She screamed again.

The other one twitched too, as if it wanted to be included in the insult.

“Oh, very funny,” she croaked, for her throat burned from the sea-witch’s potion and her voice was gone besides. “Very clever. Which of ye did this? Was it the crabs? I’ll wager it was the crabs. Nasty little pranksters, the lot of them, always scuttling sideways like they’ve a guilty conscience.”

She seized one leg with both hands and peered at the end of it. There were five small nubs.

“Toes?” she thought, horrified. “I’ve grown toes?”

She wriggled them.

They wriggled back.

The mermaid went very still.

“Well,” she thought, “that’s unnatural.”

She looked about for witnesses, but there was no one nearby except a few gulls, who had the impudent expression common to gulls everywhere, as if they’d seen worse and stolen half of it.

One gull gave a harsh cry.

“Oh, keep your opinions to yourself,” she mouthed, though no sound came. “You look like a floating cabbage with a gambling problem.”

Then the memory returned: the sea-witch’s hut, the dreadful bargain, the burning draught, the knife-like pain as her tail split and changed. The prince. The human soul. The terrible silence where her voice had been.

Her indignation softened into fear.

She placed her hands on the sand and tried to rise.

The new limbs wobbled beneath her like drunk sailors after payday.

“Ah,” she thought, collapsing at once, “so that’s the game. I’ve traded a perfectly good tail for two sticks with opinions.”

She tried again.

Pain shot through her feet—sharp, bright, and wicked—as though every grain of sand had taken up a tiny pitchfork.

Her eyes filled with tears.

But just then, along the shore, came the young prince with his attendants, strolling in the morning light. He saw her, this strange silent girl with sea-foam in her hair and sorrow in her eyes, and hurried toward her.

The little mermaid sat up as gracefully as she could manage, which was to say, not very. One leg had gone one way, the other had made independent plans, and her hair was full of shells.

The prince gazed at her in wonder.

She gazed back, unable to speak, unable to explain that she had crossed an ocean of pain to find him, and also that she strongly suspected her lower half had been assembled by committee.

He offered his hand.

She took it.

And when she stood, trembling, on those two absurd, aching, miraculous legs, she smiled through her tears.

Though privately, deep in her heart, she promised that if the crabs had had anything to do with it, there would be words.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly humorous fairy-tale retelling in which a mermaid loses her tail and discovers human legs for the first time, using colloquial slang and a narrator with a mischievous tone.
counterfactuals.output:
Once upon a time—because apparently that’s still how we’re doing this—there lived a mermaid named Maribel, who had hair like spilled ink, eyes like moonlit tide pools, and the personality of a cat trapped in a chandelier.

She was the youngest daughter of the Sea King, a damp old tyrant with a beard full of barnacles and the emotional range of a clam. Her sisters spent their days braiding pearls into their hair and singing at shipwrecks, as one does when one is pretty, bored, and technically an accessory to manslaughter.

Maribel, however, was different.

She wanted *adventure*. She wanted *freedom*. She wanted to know what shoes were and why humans kept inventing different kinds of them despite clearly only having two feet.

Most of all, she wanted to go Above.

“Absolutely not,” said the Sea King, who said this about everything, including seasoning.

“But Dad—”

“No.”

“I’m sixteen hundred tides old—”

“No.”

“I watched a sailor eat a live crab on a dare and then propose to a barrel. I think I can handle the surface.”

The Sea King’s left eyebrow twitched, dislodging a shrimp. “Humans are dangerous, foolish creatures.”

“So are sharks, and you let Uncle Garth come to dinner.”

Uncle Garth, circling in the corner, burped up a boot.

The Sea King pointed his trident at her. “Enough. You will stay where you belong.”

Now, if there is one thing fairy-tale fathers consistently fail to understand, it’s that telling a teenage girl where she belongs is basically loading a cannon and aiming it at your own throne room.

So that night, Maribel slipped out through the kelp gardens, past the sleeping eels, past the coral gates, and down into the deepest trench where even the lanternfish muttered, “Nope,” and turned around.

There lived Morvella, the Sea Witch.

Morvella was not what you’d call conventionally beautiful unless your conventions included “haunted umbrella” and “sentient pile of elbows.” She had a smile like a cracked plate and a garden of bottled screams arranged by pitch.

“Maribel,” she crooned, stirring a cauldron full of something that winked at her. “Little princess. Come to trade your voice for love? Very classic. Very stale.”

Maribel crossed her arms. “Actually, I want legs.”

Morvella blinked. “Just legs?”

“Yes.”

“No prince?”

“Ew.”

“No grand romantic tragedy?”

“I’m open to mild chaos.”

The witch sighed. “Kids these days. No respect for narrative structure.”

“I’ll pay.”

“Oh, I’m sure you will.” Morvella’s grin widened. Somewhere nearby, a skull whispered, “Red flag, babe.”

Maribel ignored it. “What do you want?”

“Your tail.”

Maribel looked down at her shimmering tail, all silver and blue, strong enough to outrun a swordfish and slap a rude dolphin into next Tuesday. “My tail?”

“Yes.”

“Like… temporarily?”

Morvella laughed so hard a few teeth escaped and had to be herded back into her mouth. “Darling, nothing good is temporary, and nothing temporary is cheap.”

Maribel hesitated.

Now, here’s the thing about mermaids: their tails are not merely decorative fish-pants. A tail is balance. Speed. Identity. Dignity. It is also very convenient for knocking over annoying siblings.

But Maribel was sixteen hundred tides old, which is old enough to make one bad decision and young enough to call it self-discovery.

“Deal,” she said.

Morvella clapped. “Love a customer with minimal survival instinct.”

The witch produced a knife made from whale bone and moonlight.

“Uh,” said Maribel. “What’s that for?”

“Oh, relax. This is a fairy tale. Pain is just character development with better lighting.”

Before Maribel could say, “Hang on, maybe I’d like to read the terms and conditions,” Morvella sliced through the water with the knife.

There was no blood.

That would have been too easy.

Instead, Maribel felt her tail unravel.

Scales peeled away like coins shaken from a purse. Her fins folded inward with a sound like wet silk tearing. Her spine cracked, politely at first, then with increasing enthusiasm, like a haunted rocking chair.

She screamed.

The bottled screams screamed back, which was honestly rude.

When it was over, Maribel floated in the witch’s grotto, pale and shivering, with two strange limbs where her tail had once been.

Legs.

Human legs.

Long, wobbly, absurdly jointed things. They ended in feet, which looked like hands that had given up on ambition.

Maribel stared at them.

One foot twitched.

She shrieked and punched it.

“Ow!” she yelled.

Morvella applauded. “Wonderful. First contact.”

“These are disgusting.”

“They’re yours.”

“They have toes.”

“Ten of them.”

“Why so many?”

“For suffering,” said Morvella cheerfully. “And dancing.”

Maribel tried to move. Her legs kicked in opposite directions like two drunk squids having a domestic dispute. She flipped upside down, smacked into a shelf, and dislodged a jar labeled *Regrets, 1832–1849*.

It shattered.

A ghostly voice sighed, “I should’ve married the baker.”

Morvella shoved Maribel toward a tunnel leading upward. “Off you go.”

“Wait! How do I use these?”

“You’ll figure it out.”

“That’s not helpful!”

“I’m a witch, not a physical therapist.”

And with that, Morvella summoned a current and launched Maribel toward the surface like a cursed champagne cork.

She shot through black water, past startled jellyfish, past a shark who looked her up and down and said, “Girl, what happened to your butt?” and finally burst through the waves onto a moonlit shore.

She landed face-first in the sand.

It was not a graceful debut.

The sea foamed around her. The wind slapped her wet hair across her face. Her new legs sprawled behind her, pale and trembling, looking less like instruments of freedom and more like two uncooked noodles someone had abandoned at a crime scene.

Maribel lifted her head.

The beach was silent.

Then a crab scuttled over.

He looked at her legs.

He looked at her face.

He said, “Yikes.”

“Shut up,” Maribel groaned.

The crab raised both claws. “Hey, I’m just an observer.”

Maribel pushed herself upright. Sitting was difficult but possible. Standing, however, appeared to be a form of witchcraft more advanced than the one that had mutilated her.

She grabbed a rock.

Her legs buckled.

She grabbed a piece of driftwood.

Her knees betrayed her.

She tried again and rose halfway, trembling heroically—then sneezed, folded like a cheap chair, and went down with a noise that made the crab wince.

“Solid effort,” he said. “Very tragic. Big fan.”

“I hate this.”

“Welcome to land. Everything’s hard and most of it has taxes.”

Maribel spat sand from her mouth. “Humans do this all the time?”

“Constantly.”

“On purpose?”

“Allegedly.”

She examined her feet again. Toes curled into the sand like pale little worms. The sensation was revolting.

Also fascinating.

The ground did not move beneath her. There was no current holding her up, no buoyant cradle of saltwater, no soft push of the deep. Here, everything was weight. Gravity clung to her bones like a needy ex.

Maribel tried standing once more.

This time, she planted her feet wide, gripped the driftwood, and hauled herself upright.

For one glorious second, she stood.

The moon shone.

The waves whispered.

The crab gasped. “No way.”

Maribel grinned.

Then she took her first step.

Her foot landed sideways. Her ankle made a noise like a twig reconsidering life. She windmilled her arms, shouted a word princesses are not supposed to know, and crashed into a pile of seaweed.

The crab nodded. “Nailed it.”

Maribel lay there, staring at the stars.

A strange feeling bubbled up inside her.

Not regret.

Not quite.

It was too sharp for regret. Too alive.

She had lost her tail. Her home. Her place in the water. She had gained pain, sand in every conceivable crevice, and a pair of legs that seemed personally committed to her downfall.

And yet—

She laughed.

It started small, then grew wild and ugly and bright, until gulls woke and complained in the distance.

The crab backed away. “Okay, that’s unsettling.”

Maribel sat up, seaweed draped over her head like a drowned duchess. “I did it.”

“You fell.”

“I left.”

“You also fell.”

“I have legs.”

“Bad ones.”

“They’re new.”

“They’re haunted.”

She flexed her toes. They wriggled horribly. She loved them immediately.

By dawn, Maribel had learned three things.

First: walking was less like swimming and more like repeatedly stopping yourself from eating dirt.

Second: humans had invented clothing because skin was apparently always too cold, too hot, too visible, or too likely to get arrested.

Third: legs were not freedom.

They were tools.

Awkward, painful, ridiculous tools.

Freedom was deciding what to do after you’d made a spectacular mess of yourself.

So when the first humans found her on the beach—a fisherman, his wife, and their snotty little child carrying a bucket of doomed clams—Maribel did not sing a tragic ballad or beg for a prince.

She stood, wobbling, naked except for seaweed and spite.

The fisherman dropped his net.

His wife crossed herself.

The child pointed. “Mama, why’s that lady walking like Grandpa after cider?”

Maribel smiled with all the sweetness of a shark in a bonnet.

“I require pants,” she announced.

And because fairy tales are very particular about fate, destiny, and dramatic timing, the fisherman’s wife happened to be kind, practical, and exactly the sort of woman who saw a naked sea-girl emerge from the ocean and thought, *Well, somebody’s got to sort this nonsense out.*

She wrapped Maribel in a cloak and led her inland.

Behind them, the crab watched from the surf.

“You forgot your whole fish situation!” he called.

Maribel turned back.

For just a moment, she saw the sea glittering under the morning sun. Her father’s kingdom waited beneath it. Her sisters. Her past. Her tail, perhaps bottled now in Morvella’s horrible collection, labeled *Princess, impulsive, lightly used*.

Her chest ached.

Then her knees wobbled.

She nearly toppled into the fisherman.

The crab sighed. “Yeah, okay. Bigger problems.”

Maribel faced the road ahead.

It curved into forests, villages, taverns, graveyards, markets, heartbreaks, bad soup, worse men, sharp stones, warm fires, and shoes.

Especially shoes.

Her feet curled in anticipation or fear. Hard to tell. They were new and dramatic.

“Well,” she said, gripping the cloak around her shoulders, “let’s see what kind of trouble these ugly little land-forks can get me into.”

And off she went—stumbling, swearing, laughing—into the human world.

Not graceful.

Not saved.

Not even remotely prepared.

But upright.

Mostly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary pastiche about the Little Mermaid’s transformation into a woman, emphasizing grotesque physical comedy, confusion about her new limbs, and wordplay around “legless.”
counterfactuals.output:
When first the little mermaid found herself ashore, she discovered that mankind had been greatly overpraised in the matter of walking.

The sea had never required such arrangements. One did not, in polite coral society, split oneself into a pair of pink stilts and then attempt to balance a heart, a stomach, and a bewildered head upon them. Yet there they were: two long, pale, contrary things, hinged in the middle like folding oars, and ending in five small sea-anemones apiece.

“Toes,” she thought, with horror. “Why so many?”

She lifted one foot. The other, offended by this favoritism, gave way at once, and she sat down in the sand with a sound like a sack of wet laundry being dropped by a cook in a hurry. A crab, who had been minding his own business, applauded with both claws.

The mermaid tried again. First she commanded the right leg to proceed. It did, but too enthusiastically, flinging itself forward as though it intended to leave without the rest of her. The left leg, not to be outdone, tangled itself behind it. Her knees knocked together like two frightened clams, and she pitched face-first into a ribbon of seaweed.

A fisherman’s boy, seeing her struggle upright, cried, “Poor maid! She is legless!”

This seemed unfair. She had never been more legged in her life.

Indeed, leglessness had been simple: a noble silver tail, a single splendid sweep, one thought and away. But now she was burdened with a surplus of leg. Legful. Leg-laden. Leg-bedeviled. If this was what the landfolk meant by getting ahead, she felt they had neglected the lower half of the argument.

She took a step. Pain flashed through her soles like walking upon broken moonlight. She opened her mouth to cry out, but no voice came—only a soundless gasp, elegant and tragic, immediately spoiled by the fact that her new knees had bent the wrong way and deposited her into a dune.

There she lay, hair full of sand, dignity leaking out of her like water from a cracked pail.

A gull regarded her with professional contempt.

“Laugh if you like,” she tried to say, but of course she could not. The bargain had stolen her speech, leaving her with only expressions, gestures, and two legs which seemed determined to make up the difference by speaking nonsense with every joint.

She pointed at her feet accusingly.

The feet pointed back, ten toes wriggling in innocent astonishment.

At last she rose again, wobbling like a candle in a storm. One step. Then another. The world tilted, lurched, steadied. Her ankles trembled; her calves quivered; her heels sank; her toes clutched the sand with the desperation of small, naked starfish.

The prince’s palace gleamed far away.

The sea whispered behind her, smooth and indivisible.

Before her stretched the long road of humankind: hard, bright, ridiculous—and requiring, she now understood, a great deal of legwork.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of a modern Irish storyteller, narrate the moment a mermaid wakes after magic has given her legs, with crude humor, odd metaphors, and a melancholy final line.
counterfactuals.output:
She woke on the strand with the dawn chewing pink at the edge of the world, and for a while she thought the sea had played one of its usual jokes on her—rolled her in sleep, filled her ears with sand, and left her mouth tasting like a drowned priest’s sock.

Then she tried to flick her tail.

Nothing flicked.

Below her belly, where once there’d been a fine silver sweep of scale and muscle, good enough to shame moonlight itself, there were two long pale things lying there in the wrack like a pair of badly peeled eels. They had knees, God help her. Knees! Little knobbly hinges halfway down, as if some drunk carpenter had been asked to build a fish and had given up after the second bottle.

She stared.

One of the things twitched.

She screamed so loud a gull dropped a crab out of sheer respect.

“What in the holy arse of the abyss is that?” she cried, though there was nobody near but the stones, and stones are terrible for conversation unless you’ve the patience of a saint or the intelligence of a limpet.

She poked one leg with a finger. It was hers. She felt it. Felt the poke, felt the cold, felt a miserable itch on the shin like a tiny devil with a rake. Then came the feet—two flat, ugly paddles at the ends, each sprouting five small pale worms. Toes, they were called in the witch’s bargain. Toes, like an afterthought. Like punctuation at the end of a bad sentence.

She tried to sit up and immediately discovered the world had changed its rules. The old body had been music: one sweep, one curve, one glorious answer to the water. This new arrangement was a committee meeting in a sack. Everything bent the wrong way or too much or not enough. Her hips complained. Her calves pulled. Her backside, never before consulted in matters of travel, made itself known with a damp slap against the sand.

“Ah, lovely,” she muttered. “A hole for shite and no clue how to steer it.”

The first step was less a step than a betrayal. She rose, wobbled, flapped both arms like a saint being electrocuted, and went face-first into a heap of bladderwrack. The seaweed burst under her with a noise like an old man farting in chapel.

From the shallows, the waves came whispering in. They licked her ankles—ankles! another ridiculous invention—and retreated, as if embarrassed to see her so reduced. She wanted to laugh. She wanted to vomit. She wanted to bite the witch’s nose off and spit it into a lobster pot.

But then she looked inland.

There were fields beyond the dunes, grey-green and soft under the morning mist. A chimney smoking. A road curling away like a question asked by someone afraid of the answer. Somewhere up there was the man with the warm hands and the sad songs, the one who’d made the surface seem less like exile and more like a door.

So she stood again.

The legs shook beneath her, foolish and faithful. She took one step. Then another. Each hurt like a curse learning her name.

Behind her, the tide sighed over the place where her tail had been, and the sea went on calling her darling in a language she could no longer answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short, surreal monologue retelling the Little Mermaid’s first morning on land, where she mistakes her new legs for strange objects before her sister explains them.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, I woke on the sand with two pale oars tied to my heart.

They lay where my tail had been—long, jointed, absurd things, like candles that had forgotten how to melt. I tried to swim with them, but they only kicked the morning. I thought perhaps the sea witch had given me a pair of stranded eels, or white branches from a drowned tree, or two quiet lightning bolts waiting for thunder.

When I touched them, they answered with pain.

I wept into the shore until my sister rose from the foam, her hair full of pearls and warning.

“Those are legs,” she said softly. “Humans stand on them.”

“Stand?” I asked. “Like a mast? Like a gull on a rock?”

“Like a wish pretending it is not falling.”

She took my hands and lifted me. The world rushed upward. The beach sharpened beneath me. Every grain of sand became a tiny tooth.

And so I stood—on my two impossible questions—while the sea behind me called and called my old name.
